result.overall: The application for judicial review is allowed because the Officer breached procedural fairness by not giving the applicant an opportunity to address concerns about the credibility of his employment letter.

themes.name: Procedural fairness duty
themes.summary: Whether the Officer breached procedural fairness by failing to provide the applicant an opportunity to address concerns about the credibility of his employment letter.

themes.name: Sufficiency vs credibility of evidence
themes.summary: Distinguishing whether the Officer's concerns related to the sufficiency of evidence or the credibility/veracity of the employment letter, which affects procedural fairness obligations.

themes.name: Assessment of employment letter
themes.summary: Evaluation of the employment letter's content, its mirroring of the NOC duties, and whether it was self-serving or credible evidence of work experience.

themes.name: Standards of review
themes.summary: Correctness standard applies to procedural fairness issues; reasonableness standard applies to eligibility and evidence assessment.

arguments.quote: On January 27, 2012, his application was refused at the screening stage by the Canadian High Commission in London because the visa officer (the Officer) found that the applicant had not provided sufficient independent documentation demonstrating his experience as a general practitioner or family physician. In her letter refusing eligibility, the Officer indicated that she was not satisfied that the applicant was a general practitioner or family physician because he failed to provide sufficient independent documentation demonstrating his experience.
arguments.claim: The visa officer refused Mr Hamza's application at the screening stage because he did not provide sufficient independent documentation to demonstrate his experience as a general practitioner or family physician.

arguments.quote: Although the NOC code(s) correspond(s) to the occupations specified in the Instructions, the main duties that you listed do not indicate that you performed the actions described in the lead statement for the occupation, as set out in the occupational descriptions of the NOC, or that you performed all of the essential duties and a substantial number of the main duties, as set out in the occupational descriptions of the NOC.
arguments.claim: The officer found that the duties Mr Hamza listed did not indicate he performed the lead statement actions or all essential duties required by the NOC for his occupation.

arguments.quote: Since you did not provide satisfactory evidence that you have work experience in any of the listed occupations, you do not meet the requirements of the Ministerial Instructions and your application is not eligible for processing.
arguments.claim: The officer concluded that Mr Hamza did not meet the requirements of the Ministerial Instructions and was therefore ineligible for processing.

arguments.quote: The Officer’s Computerized Assisted Immigration Processing System (CAIPS) notes, which form part of the Officer’s decision (Taleb v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 384 at para 25, 407 FTR 185), capture in more detail the reasoning that led the Officer to reject Mr Hamza’s application at the selection stage: Applicant has provided only two references to demonstrate his experience. One is prepared by himself and the other is prepared by the office of the medical Sup. This reference appears to be prepared for this application and therefore is self serving. There are no other supporting documents to demonstrate his employment as a physician and therefore his application is refused at screening.
arguments.claim: The officer's notes indicated that Mr Hamza provided only two references: one self-prepared and one from the medical superintendent's office, which appeared self-serving and lacked other supporting documents.

arguments.quote: The first issue relates to procedural fairness: Did the Officer breach her duty of procedural fairness by not providing the applicant with an opportunity to address her concerns regarding the applicant’s employment letter?
arguments.claim: The Officer breached her duty of procedural fairness by not providing the applicant an opportunity to address concerns about the employment letter.
arguments.outcome_note: Issue raised by the application for determination.

arguments.quote: The second issue raised by this application is whether it was reasonably open for the Officer to conclude, on the basis of the evidence submitted by the applicant, that he had not satisfactorily established his work experience as a family physician.
arguments.claim: It was not reasonably open for the Officer to conclude that the applicant had not satisfactorily established his work experience as a family physician based on the evidence submitted.
arguments.outcome_note: Issue raised by the application for determination.

arguments.quote: The parties are in agreement as to the appropriate standards of review.
arguments.claim: The parties agree on the appropriate standards of review.

arguments.quote: It included an allegation that the Officer had blindly and unreasonably relied on a check-list to reject the applicant’s certificate where he listed his duties when working at his own clinic because it was not corroborated by third-party documentation. However, at the hearing, counsel for the applicant informed me that the applicant was no longer pursuing this argument and was relying solely on the remaining arguments presented in his written submissions relating to the employment letter.
arguments.claim: The applicant initially alleged that the Officer unreasonably relied on a checklist to reject the applicant's certificate listing his duties at his own clinic due to lack of third-party corroboration.
arguments.outcome_note: Applicant abandoned this argument at the hearing

arguments.quote: Essentially, the applicant argues that it was unreasonable and an abuse of process for the Officer not to give any weight to the employment letter from the applicant’s supervisor for the simple fact that it mirrors the NOC description.
arguments.claim: The applicant argues it was unreasonable and an abuse of process for the Officer to give no weight to the employment letter from his supervisor simply because it mirrored the NOC description.

arguments.quote: Further, the applicant contends that the CAIPS notes reveal that the Officer’s concerns were related to the credibility and veracity of the employment letter, as opposed to the sufficiency of the documentation that he provided.
arguments.claim: The applicant contends that the Officer's concerns were about the credibility and veracity of the employment letter, not the sufficiency of the documentation provided.

arguments.quote: In this regard, the applicant insists that it is normal that the employment letter was “prepared for this application” and was “self-serving” since it was specifically provided to comply with the requirements set out in the check-list.
arguments.claim: The applicant insists it is normal that the employment letter was prepared for the application and was self-serving, as it was provided to meet checklist requirements.

arguments.quote: He also insists that the letter is both independent and objective, as it was prepared by a government officer.
arguments.claim: The applicant insists the employment letter is independent and objective because it was prepared by a government officer.

arguments.quote: In addition, the applicant contends that the CAIPS notes clearly suggest that the Officer was not questioning the sufficiency of the evidence provided, but rather, its credibility.
arguments.claim: The applicant contends the CAIPS notes suggest the Officer questioned the credibility of the evidence, not its sufficiency.

arguments.quote: Therefore, the applicant argues that the Officer should have provided him with an opportunity to address her concerns.
arguments.claim: The applicant argues the Officer should have given him an opportunity to address her concerns about the employment letter.

arguments.quote: By failing to do so, the Officer breached her duty of procedural fairness.
arguments.claim: By failing to provide an opportunity to address concerns, the Officer breached her duty of procedural fairness.

arguments.quote: The applicant contends that this principle has been recognized in the jurisprudence and he relies mainly on Patel v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 571 at paras 20-27 (available on CanLII) [Patel] and on Hassani v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1283 at paras 23-24, [2007] 3 FCR 501 [Hassani].
arguments.claim: The applicant relies on jurisprudence recognizing the duty of procedural fairness, mainly Patel v Canada and Hassani v Canada.

arguments.quote: At the hearing, counsel for the applicant stated that he acknowledged that in Obeta v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 1542 (available on CanLII) [Obeta], Justice Boivin departed from this principle, but he insisted that the circumstances in Obeta were totally different from those in this case.
arguments.claim: At the hearing, counsel acknowledged that Obeta departed from this principle but argued the circumstances in Obeta differ from this case.

arguments.quote: The respondent argues that the Officer’s decision is reasonable, and that the Officer did not breach the applicant’s right to procedural fairness.
arguments.claim: The Officer’s decision is reasonable and did not breach the applicant’s right to procedural fairness.

arguments.quote: The respondent contends that the Officer did not question the credibility of the evidence provided by the applicant, but was concerned with the sufficiency of that evidence.
arguments.claim: The Officer did not question the credibility of the evidence but was concerned with its sufficiency.

arguments.quote: The respondent submits that one could not infer from the indication that the employment letter was “self-serving”, that the Officer thought that the letter was fraudulent.
arguments.claim: The indication that the employment letter was 'self-serving' does not mean the Officer thought the letter was fraudulent.

arguments.quote: In the respondent’s view, the employment letter was clearly insufficient and should have contained a detailed description of the applicant’s duties and responsibilities.
arguments.claim: The employment letter was clearly insufficient and should have contained a detailed description of the applicant’s duties and responsibilities.

arguments.quote: Further, the respondent submits that the letter is not disinterested evidence as it advocates for a particular position by copying elements from the NOC, instead of providing a detailed description of the applicant’s tasks.
arguments.claim: The employment letter is not disinterested evidence as it advocates for a particular position by copying elements from the NOC instead of providing a detailed description of the applicant’s tasks.

arguments.quote: The respondent argues that it was reasonable, in the circumstances, for the Officer to give little weight to a letter merely mirroring the NOC.
arguments.claim: It was reasonable for the Officer to give little weight to a letter merely mirroring the NOC.

arguments.quote: Further, the respondent submits that when the evidence provided in support of an application is insufficient, a visa officer is not required to inform the applicant of his or her concerns before making a negative determination.
arguments.claim: When evidence is insufficient, a visa officer is not required to inform the applicant of concerns before making a negative determination.

arguments.quote: The respondent suggests that the circumstances in Patel, above, are distinguishable as it was clear in that case that the officer’s concerns were related to the authenticity of the evidence, which is not the case here.
arguments.claim: The circumstances in Patel are distinguishable because the officer’s concerns there related to authenticity, which is not the case here.

arguments.quote: In the alternative, the respondent relies on Obeta, above, to establish that even if the Court is of the view that the Officer’s concerns were related to the credibility of the employment letter, it does not establish that the Officer had an obligation to provide the applicant with an opportunity to address these concerns.
arguments.claim: Even if the Officer’s concerns were about the credibility of the employment letter, there was no obligation to provide the applicant an opportunity to address these concerns, relying on Obeta.

arguments.quote: The respondent also relied on Kamchibekov v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 1411 (available on CanLII) [Kamchibekov].
arguments.claim: The respondent also relied on Kamchibekov v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 1411.

arguments.quote: Karachi dated 14/11/9 which is covering experience from June 1988 to date and the Job duties mirror NOC description. This reference appears to be prepared for this application and therefore is self serving.
arguments.claim: The visa officer had concerns about the employment letter's credibility because it mirrored the NOC description and appeared self-serving.

arguments.quote: In the case at bar, the applicant provided two documents to establish his work experience: a self-declared certificate describing the duties that he performs when he works at his own clinic and an employment letter from Dr Harroon, the Medical Superintendent of the hospital. In the employment letter, the Medical Superintendent unequivocally indicated that the applicant has been working at the Government Hospital of Karachi as a family physician, and that he has been performing the duties listed in the letter.
arguments.claim: The applicant provided an employment letter from the Medical Superintendent attesting to his duties as a family physician.

arguments.quote: The employment letter states that the applicant has been performing the following duties: • Prescribe and administer medications and treatments. • Provide emergency care. • Inoculate and vaccinate patients. • Provide acute care management. • Provide emergency care. • Advise patients and their families on health care including health promotion, disease, illness and accident prevention. • Examine patients and take their histories, order laboratory tests, X‑rays and other diagnostic procedures and consult with other medical practitioners to evaluate patients’ physical and mental health. Had the Officer been satisfied that the duties listed in the employment letter were actually the duties performed by the applicant, then, there would be no reason, considering that these duties correspond to the main duties set out in the NOC, for the Officer to find this evidence to be insufficient.
arguments.claim: The employment letter accurately lists the main duties performed by the applicant, corresponding to the NOC 3112 description.

arguments.quote: There is no rule that requires an applicant to provide more than one employment letter to establish sufficient work experience.
arguments.claim: There is no rule requiring more than one employment letter to establish sufficient work experience.

arguments.quote: An application can be deemed complete even if the work experience is supported by a single employment letter, as long as the employment letter accurately and completely lists the main duties performed by the applicant.
arguments.claim: An application can be complete with a single employment letter if it accurately and completely lists the main duties performed.

arguments.quote: This reference appears to be prepared for this application and therefore is self serving. There are no other supporting documents to demonstrate his employment as a physician and therefore his application is refused at screening.
arguments.claim: The officer found the employment letter self-serving and insufficient without other supporting documents, leading to refusal at screening.

holdings.quote: Mr Hamza (the applicant or Mr Hamza) is a citizen of Pakistan. He submitted an application for permanent residence in Canada in the Federal Skilled Worker class as a family physician.
holdings.statement: Mr Hamza is a citizen of Pakistan who applied for permanent residence in Canada as a Federal Skilled Worker in the occupation of family physician.

holdings.quote: He included his wife and three children in his application.
holdings.statement: Mr Hamza included his wife and three children in his application for permanent residence.

holdings.quote: Subsection 75(2) of the Regulations defines the skilled worker as a person who has at least one year of continuous full-time employment experience in one of the listed occupations of the National Occupational Classification (NOC) within the last 10 years. In order to be recognized as a skilled worker, a person must establish that during that period of employment, he or she performed the actions described in the lead statement of the NOC for the relevant position and a substantial number of the main duties as set out in the NOC, including all of the essential duties (paragraphs 75(2)(b) and (c)).
holdings.statement: The Federal Skilled Worker class requires applicants to demonstrate at least one year of continuous full-time employment in a listed occupation and to have performed the essential duties described in the National Occupational Classification (NOC).

holdings.quote: The occupation of “general practitioner and family physician” is described in NOC 3112.
holdings.statement: The occupation of general practitioner and family physician is described in NOC 3112.

holdings.quote: In schedule 1 of his application form, the applicant indicated that he has been working as a family physician, both at his privately owned clinic and at the Sindh Governmental Hospital in Karachi since 1988.
holdings.statement: Mr Hamza claimed to have worked as a family physician since 1988 at his own clinic and at the Sindh Governmental Hospital in Karachi.

holdings.quote: To establish his work experience, he provided a self-declared certificate, attesting that he had been practicing as a family physician at his clinic since 1988 and setting out his main duties and responsibilities. He also filed a letter, dated November 14, 2009, from Dr Imtiaz Haroon, Medical Superintendent of the Sindh Government Hospital of Liaquatabad in Karachi (the employment letter), attesting that the applicant has been working in their organization as a family physician since 1988. Dr Haroon also listed the applicant’s major responsibilities, which mirror several duties listed in the NOC 3112.
holdings.statement: To establish his work experience, Mr Hamza provided a self-declared certificate and a letter from Dr Imtiaz Haroon, Medical Superintendent of the Sindh Government Hospital, attesting to his work as a family physician since 1988 and listing his duties.

holdings.quote: The employment letter ends with a comment from the Superintendent stating that the applicant is “very co-operative, hard working and a dedicated doctor”. In addition, the Superintendent noted that the certificate was being issued at the applicant’s request.
holdings.statement: The employment letter included a positive comment about Mr Hamza's character and noted it was issued at his request.

holdings.quote: This issue requires the Court to determine, first, if the Officer’s concerns were related to the credibility of the employment letter provided by the applicant, or to the sufficiency of the evidence provided.
holdings.statement: The Court must determine if the Officer's concerns were about the credibility of the employment letter or the sufficiency of the evidence provided.

holdings.quote: Second, if the Court is satisfied that the Officer’s concerns were related to the veracity of the employment letter, it must determine whether, in the circumstances of this case, the Officer should have provided the applicant with an opportunity to address her concerns.
holdings.statement: If the Officer's concerns were about the veracity of the employment letter, the Court must decide whether the Officer should have given the applicant an opportunity to address those concerns.

holdings.quote: No deference is accorded to the Officer’s decision regarding issues of procedural fairness and, therefore, the first issue is reviewable on a correctness standard of review (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 43, [2009] 1 SCR 339; Sketchley v Canada (Attorney General), 2005 FCA 404 at para 53, [2006] 3 FCR 392;
holdings.statement: No deference is given to the Officer's decision on procedural fairness issues, which are reviewed on a correctness standard.

holdings.quote: However, the Officer’s analysis of the applicant’s eligibility for permanent residence as a Federal Skilled Worker involves an assessment of the evidence and the exercise of discretion and is reviewable on the reasonableness standard of review (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, [2008] 1 SCR 190; Zhu, above at para 23;
holdings.statement: The Officer's assessment of eligibility for permanent residence as a Federal Skilled Worker involves evidence assessment and discretion, reviewed on a reasonableness standard.

holdings.quote: First, the onus clearly falls on the applicant to establish that he or she meets the requirements of the Regulations by providing sufficient evidence in support of his or her application (El Sherbiny v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 69 at para 6 (available on CanLII) [El Sherbiny]; Enriquez, above at para 8; Torres, above at paras 37-40; Kaur v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 758 at para 30 (available on CanLII) [Kaur]; Oladipo v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2008 FC 366 at para 24, 166 ACWS (3d) 355; Ismaili, above, at para 18.
holdings.statement: The onus is on the applicant to provide sufficient evidence to meet the requirements of the Regulations for permanent residence applications.

holdings.quote: Second, the duty of procedural fairness owed by visa officers is on the low end of the spectrum (Farooq v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 164 at para 10 (available on CanLII) [Farooq]; Sandhu, above at para 25; Trivedi v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, 2010 FC 422 at para 39 (available on CanLII) [Trivedi]; Khan v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2001 FCA 345 at paras 30-32, [2002] 2 FC 413; Patel v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2002 FCA 55 at para 10, 288 NR 48; Chiau v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) (2000), [2001] 2 FC 297 at para 41 (available on CanLII) (CA), leave to appeal to SCC refused, 28418 (August 16, 2001).
holdings.statement: The duty of procedural fairness owed by visa officers is low in the context of permanent residence applications.

holdings.quote: Third, a visa officer has neither an obligation to notify an applicant of inadequacies in his or her application nor in the material provided in support of the application. Furthermore, a visa officer has no obligation to seek clarification or additional documentation, or to provide an applicant with an opportunity to address his or her concerns, when the material provided in support of an application is unclear, incomplete or insufficient to convince the officer that the applicant meets all the requirements that stem from the Regulations (Hassani, above at paras 23-24; Patel, above at para 21; El Sherbiny, above at para 6; Sandhu, above at para, 25; Luongo v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 618 at para 18 (available on CanLII); Ismaili, above at para 18; Triveldi, above at para 42; Singh, above at para 40;
holdings.statement: Visa officers have no obligation to notify applicants of inadequacies, seek clarification, or provide an opportunity to address concerns when the evidence is unclear, incomplete, or insufficient.

holdings.quote: Nevertheless, a duty to provide an applicant with the opportunity to respond to an officer’s concerns may arise when the officer is concerned with the credibility, the veracity, or the authenticity of the documentation provided by an applicant as opposed to the sufficiency of the evidence provided.
holdings.statement: A duty to provide an opportunity to respond arises only when the officer's concerns relate to credibility, veracity, or authenticity of the documentation, not mere sufficiency of evidence.

holdings.quote: In this case, the first issue to be determined is whether the Officer’s concerns were related to the sufficiency or to the credibility of the evidence submitted by the applicant to establish his work experience.
holdings.statement: The first issue is whether the Officer's concerns related to sufficiency or credibility of the applicant's evidence regarding work experience.

holdings.quote: A visa officer may have raised concerns about the credibility of an applicant’s documentary evidence even though he or she did not express an explicit credibility finding. Visa officers’ decisions must be analysed as a whole and in the context of the specific facts of each case. As stated by Justice Mosley in Adeoye v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 680 at para 8, 216 ACWS (3d) 191: “Although the officer did not make any explicit credibility findings, his scepticism about the applicant’s claim and supporting documents is apparent from the decision.” The same may apply in this case,
holdings.statement: Visa officers' decisions must be analyzed as a whole and in context; concerns about credibility may be implied even without explicit findings.

holdings.quote: I find it difficult to conclude that the Officer’s concerns did not relate to the credibility of the employment letter. In my view, by stating that the employment letter is self-serving, the Officer is saying that she doubts the veracity of its content.
holdings.statement: The officer's concerns related to the credibility of the employment letter and its self-serving nature, implying doubt about its veracity.

holdings.quote: I cannot say that it was unreasonable for the Officer to wonder whether the employment letter accurately reflected the applicant’s duties and responsibilities.
holdings.statement: It was not unreasonable for the officer to question whether the employment letter accurately reflected the applicant's duties and responsibilities.

holdings.quote: However, in my view, she should have allowed the applicant an opportunity to address her concerns before rendering her decision.
holdings.statement: The officer should have allowed the applicant an opportunity to address her concerns before making a decision.

holdings.quote: This case is distinguishable from the case in Kaur v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 442 (available on CanLII), where the employment letter failed to include any information regarding the duties performed by the applicant and was limited to stating that the applicant was “a good worker and had learned to cook many types of Indian meals” (at para 3). In that case, the Court found that the applicant failed to provide sufficient evidence in support of her application and that, in light of this insufficient evidence, the visa officer was not required to advise her of the inadequacy of her material. In this case, the employment letter did list the duties performed by the applicant.
holdings.statement: The case is distinguishable from Kaur, where the employment letter lacked any information on duties and the officer was not required to advise the applicant of inadequacies.

holdings.quote: One must keep in mind that every case is fact-driven.
holdings.statement: Every case is fact-driven and must be considered on its own facts.

holdings.quote: In this case, the Officer was not satisfied with the employment letter because she found it to be self-serving and the job duties described mirrored the NOC description.
holdings.statement: In this case, the Officer was not satisfied with the employment letter because she found it self-serving and the job duties described mirrored the NOC description.

holdings.quote: This is not the case here. It cannot be said that the employment letter is, on its face, fabricated or otherwise void of any credibility.
holdings.statement: This case is distinguishable from Obeta because the employment letter is not on its face fabricated or void of credibility.

holdings.quote: Therefore, for the reasons set out above, I am of the view that the Officer had a duty to provide the applicant with an opportunity to address her concerns and that, by failing to do so, she breached the applicant’s right to procedural fairness.
holdings.statement: The Officer had a duty to provide the applicant an opportunity to address her concerns and by failing to do so breached the applicant’s right to procedural fairness.

holdings.quote: This conclusion is sufficient to dispose of the application, and there is no need for me to determine whether the Officer’s decision is reasonable.
holdings.statement: The conclusion reached is sufficient to dispose of the application without determining whether the Officer's decision is reasonable.

holdings.quote: The parties did not submit questions for certification, and this case does not raise serious questions of general importance.
holdings.statement: The parties did not submit questions for certification, and the case does not raise serious questions of general importance.

authorities.quote: No deference is accorded to the Officer’s decision regarding issues of procedural fairness and, therefore, the first issue is reviewable on a correctness standard of review (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 43, [2009] 1 SCR 339; Sketchley v Canada (Attorney General), 2005 FCA 404 at para 53, [2006] 3 FCR 392; Zhu v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 155 at para 22 (available on CanLII) [Zhu]; Enriquez v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 1091 at para 6 (available on CanLII)[Enriquez]; Sandhu v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 759 at para 23, 371 FTR 239 [Sandhu]; Singh v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 1306 at para 36, 95 Imm. L.R. (3d) 83; Talpur v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 25 at para 20, 210 ACWS (3d) 765 [Talpur]).
authorities.authority: The correctness standard for procedural fairness issues is supported by Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at para 43, Sketchley v Canada (Attorney General), 2005 FCA 404 at para 53, Zhu v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 155 at para 22, Enriquez v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 1091 at para 6, Sandhu v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 759 at para 23, Singh v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2010 FC 1306 at para 36, and Talpur v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 25 at para 20.

authorities.quote: However, the Officer’s analysis of the applicant’s eligibility for permanent residence as a Federal Skilled Worker involves an assessment of the evidence and the exercise of discretion and is reviewable on the reasonableness standard of review (Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, [2008] 1 SCR 190; Zhu, above at para 23; Rashed v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 175 at para 44 (available on CanLII); Enriquez, above at para 4; Ismaili v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 351 at para 10 (available on CanLII)[Ismaili]; Torres v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 818 at para 26, 2 Imm. L.R. (4th) 57 [Torres]).
authorities.authority: The reasonableness standard for eligibility assessment is supported by Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9, Zhu, Rashed v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 175 at para 44, Enriquez, Ismaili v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 351 at para 10, and Torres v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 818 at para 26.

authorities.quote: The judgments rendered by Justice Mosley in Rukmangathan v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 284, 247 FTR 147 [Rukmangathan] and Hassani, above, are often cited as being authoritative on this issue. In Rukmangathan, Justice Mosley enunciated the principle and its limits:
authorities.authority: The principles and limits of procedural fairness duties in immigration cases are authoritatively set out in Rukmangathan and Hassani by Justice Mosley.

authorities.quote: Two years later, he reiterated the principle in Hassani, in the following terms:
authorities.authority: Justice Mosley reiterated the principle regarding procedural fairness duties in Hassani.

authorities.quote: Justice Snider provided a good summary of the applicable principles in Enriquez, above, and insisted that to trigger a duty to provide an opportunity to respond to an officer’s concerns, the applicant must first provide an application that is complete:
authorities.authority: Justice Snider summarized that to trigger a duty to provide an opportunity to respond, the applicant must first provide a complete application.

authorities.quote: The context of the case at bar is somewhat similar to that in Patel, above, where the applicant provided only a single employment document in which the job duties were largely copied from the NOC. Justice O’Keefe found that the officer’s concerns were related to the veracity of the employment letter and that the officer should have offered the applicant an opportunity to address his concerns.
authorities.authority: The case is somewhat similar to Patel, where the officer should have offered the applicant an opportunity to address concerns about the employment letter's veracity.

authorities.quote: In Talpur, above, the visa officer also expressed concerns about an employment attestation that mirrored the duties set out in the NOC. The officer’s concerns were clearly stated as relating to the credibility of the letter, but the applicant had been invited to reply to the officer’s concerns during an interview. Therefore, the Court concluded that the officer had not breached the principles of natural justice given that the applicant was “afforded a reasonable opportunity to make her case or to demonstrate the genuineness of her application” (at para 22).
authorities.authority: In Talpur, the officer's concerns about the employment attestation's credibility were addressed by inviting the applicant to reply, so no breach of natural justice occurred.

authorities.quote: In Kamchibekov, above, Justice Pinard found that there was no duty on the visa officer to offer the applicant an opportunity to disabuse him of his concerns because the employment letter mirrored the duties set out in the NOC.
authorities.authority: In Kamchibekov, Justice Pinard found no duty on the visa officer to offer the applicant an opportunity to disabuse him of concerns because the employment letter mirrored the duties set out in the NOC.

authorities.quote: Justice Pinard was of the view that the evidence provided by the applicant was ambiguous and insufficient.
authorities.authority: Justice Pinard viewed the evidence provided by the applicant as ambiguous and insufficient.

authorities.quote: In Kamchibekov, the applicant had applied to be accepted in the category of Restaurant and Food Service Manager. The NOC for that position provided very generic duties and the letter of employment mirrored those generic duties.
authorities.authority: In Kamchibekov, the applicant applied in the category of Restaurant and Food Service Manager, with generic duties in the NOC mirrored by the employment letter.

authorities.quote: Furthermore, there was no indication in the officer’s letter that his concerns were related to the veracity of the letter and the decision was limited to stating that the applicant had not provided satisfactory evidence of his work experience.
authorities.authority: There was no indication in the officer’s letter that concerns related to the veracity of the letter; the decision stated the applicant had not provided satisfactory evidence of work experience.

authorities.quote: This case can also be distinguished from Obeta, above. In that case, the Court concluded that there was no absolute obligation on the officer to allow the applicant an opportunity to respond to credibility concerns that he had in a context where the application was, on its face, void of credibility because the employment letter was likely fabricated.
authorities.authority: In Obeta, the Court concluded there was no absolute obligation on the officer to allow the applicant to respond to credibility concerns where the application was on its face void of credibility because the employment letter was likely fabricated.
